name: Valerian

identity.whatItIs: An herb sold as a dietary supplement, usually as dried root, capsules, tea, or tincture.

oneLineAnswer: Valerian is a plant root sold for sleep and calm, but proof that it works is weak.
whatItDoes: Valerian is an herb: the root and underground stem of the plant Valeriana officinalis.
People have used it since ancient Greece and Rome, for poor sleep, headaches, tiredness, and stomach cramps.
Sellers today mainly promote it for sleep, nervousness, stress, and low mood.
Trials have tested it in adults with poor sleep and in children facing dental work.
NCCIH, a US government health agency, says the evidence does not yet show it helps any condition.
whatWeDoNotKnow: Nobody has clearly shown that valerian works for any health problem.
Sleep studies disagree with each other.
A 2017 US sleep-medicine guideline advised against valerian for long-term insomnia in adults.
Three small studies hint it may ease menopause symptoms, but that is thin evidence.
For anxiety, depression, premenstrual syndrome, menstrual cramps, and stress, there is not enough evidence for any conclusion.
Whether long-term use is safe, and whether it is safe while pregnant or breastfeeding, is not known.
safetyNotes: NCCIH reports that most adults have used valerian short term without apparent harm, in studies lasting up to six weeks.
Reported side effects include headache, upset stomach, mental dullness, excitability, uneasiness, and vivid dreams.
Stopping suddenly after long use has been linked to anxiety, irritability, heart rhythm changes, insomnia, and, rarely, hallucinations.
Rare liver injury has been reported, usually in people who also took other herbal products.
Because a sleep-inducing effect is possible but unproven, NCCIH says valerian should not be mixed with alcohol or sedatives.
US labels for products containing valerian often tell you to ask a health professional first if pregnant or breastfeeding, and to keep the product away from children.
Some products that list valerian are homeopathic remedies; their labels say the uses come from traditional practice and were not reviewed by the FDA.
In the US, supplements are not approved by the FDA before sale, unlike medicines.
gaps: The claim that the evidence does not yet show valerian helps any condition rests on the NCCIH article; ClinicalTrials.gov independently confirms only that valerian has been studied in trials, not the verdict on those trials.
openFDA drug labels for valerian come almost entirely from homeopathic products, so they document how valerian is marketed rather than whether it works.
No public-domain labeled human trial outcomes (result numbers, effect sizes) were found in the sources fetched; the ClinicalTrials.gov records give study design, phase, enrollment, and status only.
No grounded explanation of how valerian might act in the body was found; the fetched sources say only that a sleep-inducing effect is possible though not proven.
Nothing was grounded on interactions with named medicines, effects during pregnancy, or children's safety beyond general label warnings.
MedlinePlus has no health topic or medical-test summary that names valerian; the Insomnia topic page does not mention it.
PubChem has no compound record for valerian as a substance; it carries only the plant taxonomy record and unrelated compounds whose names come from valerian.
The NCCIH article could not be read by plain fetch (it served stylesheet code only); its text was read from the rendered page instead.
The NCCIH at-a-glance subpage returned a 404 and was not used.

evidence.claim: Valerian is a plant that is native to Europe and Asia and also grows in North America.
evidence.quote: Valerian is a plant native to Europe and Asia; it also grows in North America.

evidence.claim: The root and the underground stem, called a rhizome, are the medicinal parts.
evidence.quote: The roots and rhizomes (underground stems) of valerian are used for medicinal purposes.

evidence.claim: Its use as a medicine goes back to ancient Greece and Rome.
evidence.quote: Valerian has been used medicinally since the times of early Greece and Rome.

evidence.claim: Historical uses included insomnia, migraine, fatigue, and stomach cramps.
evidence.quote: Historically, valerian was used to treat insomnia, migraine, fatigue, and stomach cramps.

evidence.claim: Today it is promoted for insomnia, anxiety, stress, and depression.
evidence.quote: Today, valerian is promoted for insomnia, anxiety, stress, and depression.

evidence.claim: There is not enough evidence to say valerian helps any health condition.
evidence.quote: There is not enough evidence to determine whether valerian is useful for any health conditions.

evidence.claim: A 2017 guideline from the American Academy of Sleep Medicine advised against valerian for chronic insomnia in adults.
evidence.quote: the American Academy of Sleep Medicine recommended against using valerian for chronic insomnia in adults

evidence.claim: Three small studies suggest valerian might help menopause symptoms.
evidence.quote: Three small studies suggest that valerian might be helpful for menopause symptoms

evidence.claim: No conclusions can be drawn for anxiety, depression, premenstrual syndrome, menstrual cramps, or stress.
evidence.quote: not enough evidence to allow any conclusions about whether valerian is helpful for anxiety, depression, premenstrual syndrome, dysmenorrhea (menstrual cramps), stress

evidence.claim: NCCIH reports valerian is generally safe for short-term use by most adults.
evidence.quote: Research suggests that valerian is generally safe for short-term use by most adults.

evidence.claim: It has been used with apparent safety in studies of up to six weeks, at amounts recorded as 300 to 600 milligrams daily.
evidence.quote: It has been used with apparent safety in doses of 300 to 600 milligrams daily for up to 6 weeks.

evidence.claim: Safety of long-term use is unknown.
evidence.quote: The safety of long-term use of valerian is unknown.

evidence.claim: Reported side effects include headache, stomach upset, mental dullness, excitability, uneasiness, and vivid dreams.
evidence.quote: Side effects of valerian include headache, stomach upset, mental dullness, excitability, uneasiness, and vivid dreams.

evidence.claim: Stopping abruptly after chronic use has been linked to withdrawal symptoms including anxiety, irritability, heart disturbances, insomnia, and rarely hallucinations.
evidence.quote: Some may experience withdrawal symptoms, including anxiety, irritability, heart disturbances, insomnia, and in rare cases, hallucinations, if stopped abruptly after chronic use.

evidence.claim: Very rare liver injury has been reported, most often alongside other herbal products.
evidence.quote: In very rare cases, liver injury was reported when taking valerian, most often in combination with other herbals

evidence.claim: NCCIH says valerian should not be taken with alcohol or sedatives.
evidence.quote: it should not be taken along with alcohol or sedatives

evidence.claim: Little is known about safety during pregnancy or breastfeeding.
evidence.quote: Little is known about whether it’s safe to use valerian during pregnancy or while breastfeeding.

evidence.claim: In the US, dietary supplements are not approved by the FDA before they are sold.
evidence.quote: Unlike drugs, dietary supplements are not approved by the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) before they are sold to the public.

evidence.claim: The NCCIH article is public domain and is dated May 2025.
evidence.quote: This publication is not copyrighted and is in the public domain. Duplication is encouraged.

evidence.claim: A marketed homeopathic product that lists valerian carries a sleeplessness claim on its label.
evidence.quote: Indication Helps relieve occasional sleeplessness by soothing the mind, and easing you into a natural sleep.

evidence.claim: That label also states the uses rest on traditional homeopathic practice and were not FDA-reviewed.
evidence.quote: These uses are based upon traditional homeopathic practice. They have not been reviewed by the Food and Drug Administration.

evidence.claim: Another marketed product lists Valeriana officinalis 12C with the stated purpose of sleeplessness.
evidence.quote: Valeriana officinalis 12C Remedy for Sleeplessness

evidence.claim: Labels of products containing valerian include pregnancy, breastfeeding, and child-safety warnings.
evidence.quote: If pregnant or breast-feeding, ask a health professional before use. Keep out of reach of children.

evidence.claim: A US government-funded trial tested valerian for sleep in people with Parkinson's disease.
evidence.quote: The purpose of this trial is to test the short-term effectiveness of valerian, a medicinal herb, to improve sleep in patients with Parkinson's disease (PD).

evidence.claim: That Parkinson's sleep trial was Phase 2 and listed 80 participants.
